drapeaux.note: « en langue plutôt qu'en dialecte » : demande de Viking Press rapportée via Publishers Weekly (original probablement en anglais), retraduite depuis le français.

titre: The Rediscovered Ship of a 1931 Account
accroche: In 1931, Hurston completes the story of Kossola, long considered the last survivor of the Clotilda. It remains unpublished for 87 years.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1927, the anthropologist Zora Neale Hurston travels to Alabama to interview Oluale Kossola, better known as Cudjo Lewis. The man, who is about eighty-six years old, has become a sexton at a church in Africatown, a community north of Mobile. He is then, and will long remain, regarded as the last survivor of the Clotilda, the last known ship to have brought captives from Africa to the United States. The historian Hannah Durkin has since identified two other survivors, Redoshi, who died in 1937, and Matilda McCrear, who died in 1940: they outlived him, as Kossola died in 1935.

## A clandestine voyage

In the spring of 1860, Kossola, about nineteen years old, is captured in a raid carried out by the forces of Glélé, king of Dahomey, against his native region of Bantè, in present-day Benin. Taken to the slave port of Ouidah, he is sold to Captain William Foster. The importation of slaves has nevertheless been banned in the United States since January 1, 1808: Foster loads 110 captives aboard the Clotilda anyway and, once the crossing is over, burns the ship and sinks it in Mobile Bay to erase its trail. Kossola remains enslaved until the end of the Civil War, in 1865. The freed captives would like to go home but cannot raise enough money for the journey. They work, save, and buy land north of Mobile: on September 30, 1872, Kossola himself acquires about two acres for one hundred dollars. This is the beginning of Africatown.

## A manuscript rejected for its fidelity

Hurston begins her interviews with Kossola in 1927 and sees him again in 1928. According to Publishers Weekly, she returns to Plateau in 1931 for three months, and that year completes a manuscript that she wants to be faithful to her informant's language rather than to standardized English. The publisher Viking Press asks her to tell Kossola's life “in language rather than in dialect.” Hurston refuses, and the book is left without a publisher. After Hurston's death in 1960, the manuscript ends up in the archives of the Howard University library. It finally appears in 2018, under the title Barracoon, with a foreword by Alice Walker, eighty-seven years after it was completed.

## The ship catches up with the text

In January 2018, exceptionally low tides expose a wreck in the lower Mobile-Tensaw Delta, which the journalist Ben Raines believes to be the Clotilda. The lead is ruled out: the wreck comes from a ship almost twice as large. In May 2019, the Alabama Historical Commission announces that another wreck is indeed the Clotilda; the discovery had been kept secret for a year while the firm Search Inc. verified it. The ship Foster had wanted to make disappear is thus found just one year after the publication of the book that described it.

carte.punch: His publisher wanted to erase Kossola's dialect. The book did not appear until 2018.
carte.idee: In 1931, Zora Neale Hurston completes the story of Kossola, long considered the last survivor of the illegal slave trade to the United States, written in his own language rather than in standard English. It remains unpublished until 2018; a year later, the wreck of the ship it described is authenticated.

quiz.question: Why was Zora Neale Hurston's manuscript about Cudjo Lewis rejected by the publisher Viking Press?
choix: Because Hurston never finished writing the book
Because the publisher wanted to erase Kossola's dialect, which she refused
Because Hurston's archives were destroyed in a fire
Because Kossola had asked that his story appear only after his death
quiz.explication: Hurston completed the manuscript in 1931, but Viking Press wanted Kossola's life to be told in language rather than in dialect; she refused, and the book remained without a publisher until 2018. The other answers are wrong: Hurston did finish the book, no source consulted mentions a destruction of her archives (the manuscript is held at Howard University), and Kossola, according to Wikipedia, was on the contrary enthusiastic about the idea of having his name known in Africa.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Kossola and the other Clotilda captives not return to Africa after emancipation?
choix: They could not raise enough money for the journey, and bought land near Mobile
They chose to stay in order to inherit land from their former owners
The U.S. Navy forbade them to leave the country
No ship connected Alabama to West Africa anymore at that time
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The freed captives tried to raise the money for the return trip without success; they then saved up and bought land north of Mobile, where Africatown was born. Nothing indicates that they inherited land from their former masters, that an official ban held them back, or that ships were lacking.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What led to the wreck that the journalist Ben Raines believed to be the Clotilda being ruled out in 2018?
choix: It came from a ship almost twice as large as the Clotilda
It was in the Mississippi Delta, not the Mobile Delta
It lay off Ouidah, in Benin, not in Alabama
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The wreck reported in January 2018 in the lower Mobile-Tensaw Delta came from a ship almost twice as large as the Clotilda, which led to its being ruled out before the May 2019 announcement. It was located neither in the Mississippi nor in Benin.
